::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py gmm`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**How do we discover clusters without assigning labels in advance?**

A mixture model combines multiple Gaussian components. Each observation has a probability of belonging to each component; EM alternates soft assignment and weighted parameter refitting. This is likelihood-based density estimation, not necessarily a discovery of literal business categories.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
p(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal N(t\mid\mu_k,\sigma_k^2)
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

Start with component means near 10 and 20 minutes. An observation at 9 receives high responsibility for the short-time component; the M-step shifts means according to all orders' weighted memberships.

## What to pay attention to

EM may converge to a local solution. Gaussian mixtures also have variance-collapse pathologies; constrain variances and consider multiple initialisations.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
